section_title: What does it mean to remain in the true vine?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 “I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard. 2 He cuts off every branch in Me that bears no fruit, and every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes to make it even more fruitful. 3 You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you.

4 Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me. 5 I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing. 6 If anyone does not remain in Me, he is like a branch that is thrown away and withers. Such branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire, and burned.

7 If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. 8 This is to My Father’s glory, that you bear much fruit, proving yourselves to be My disciples. 9 As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love. 10 If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love, just as I have kept My Father’s commandments and remain in His love. 11 I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete.

context_lines: Jesus continues preparing the disciples for His departure with the picture of a vine and its branches. He is the true vine, the Father tends the vineyard, and the disciples are the branches. The picture centers on their dependence on Him for a fruitful life.

The Father removes fruitless branches and prunes fruitful ones for greater fruitfulness. Jesus also tells the disciples that they are already clean because of His word. The word translated prunes is καθαίρω, kathairō (kah-THY-roh). [Thayer’s lexicon](https://biblehub.com/greek/2508.htm) explains its use for cleansing a vine by pruning. The picture brings together the Father’s care, Jesus’ word and the growth He seeks.

The command to remain is μένω, menō (MEH-noh): to remain or abide. [Thayer’s entry](https://biblehub.com/greek/3306.htm) connects its use here with continuing fellowship with Christ. Jesus fills out that relationship in the passage: His words remain in the disciples, they keep His commandments and they remain in His love.

The warning about a branch that withers and is burned is serious. It stands beside the promise of fruitfulness and the assurance that Jesus wants His joy to be in them. The chapter calls for a continuing life with Him, not a moment of enthusiasm followed by independence.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians agree that fruitful life depends on Christ. They differ over whom the fruitless branches represent and what their removal and burning mean.

In a Reformed reading, [Calvin on verses 2 and 6](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/john/15.htm) understands the removed branches as people whose outward association never had a living root in Christ. The [Westminster Confession, chapter 17](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html), and the [1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 17](https://www.the1689confession.com/1689/chapter-17), teach that those truly saved will be kept by God and finally persevere, while acknowledging that they may fall into serious sin for a time. These confessions provide the wider setting for that reading; they do not speak for every Baptist.

In [Wesley’s notes on verses 4–6 and 9](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-john/), the branches are people united to Christ by living faith who must continue in that faith. He reads the warning as a real possibility of departing from that life. The Methodist [Articles of Religion, Article XII](https://www.umc.org/en/content/articles-of-religion), teach that people may depart from grace after receiving the Spirit and may, by God’s grace, repent and return.

The Catholic Church likewise teaches a real possibility of losing the state of grace through mortal sin. Its [Catechism, paragraphs 1855–1861](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_three/section_one/chapter_one/article_8/iv_the_gravity_of_sin_mortal_and_venial_sin.index.html), distinguishes this from every lesser fault: mortal sin involves grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent, and calls for repentance and God’s forgiveness. This is the doctrinal setting of the warning, not a claim that every failure means a person is cut off.

A further reading appears in [Thomas Constable’s notes on verses 2–6](https://soniclight.com/tcon/notes/html/john/john.htm). He understands the branches as believers and the warning as loss of usefulness or service, without loss of eternal salvation. He favors lifting up in verse 2. The Greek verb can have both lifting and removing senses, but [Thayer’s entry](https://biblehub.com/greek/142.htm) assigns John 15:2 to cutting away. Vocabulary alone does not settle the whole passage, and the BSB’s wording is retained here. Constable’s explanation is an individual reading, not the teaching of all churches that affirm eternal security.
god_plan_lines: The vineyard picture has a long biblical background. [Isaiah 5:1–7](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/5.htm) describes God’s vineyard, identified as Israel, and His search for justice and righteousness. Jesus’ description of Himself as the true vine provides a meaningful parallel: the fruitful life He calls for depends on remaining in Him. This connection does not by itself settle every question about Israel and the church.

[Galatians 5:22–25](https://biblehub.com/bsb/galatians/5.htm) describes the Spirit’s fruit in qualities such as love, patience and self-control. [Colossians 1:9–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/colossians/1.htm) joins knowing God’s will, good works, endurance and thanksgiving with His rescue into the Son’s kingdom. These passages help us see the kind of life God is growing, beyond a simple measure of visible success.
current_position_lines: On abiding and prayer, our study Prayer and Faith describes remaining in Christ as living in keeping with His teaching and example. Dependence on Him shapes how we live and what we desire; it is more than adding religious words to plans we have already decided to pursue. In its discussion of John 15:7, the study understands asking as being shaped by His word and will. This position concerns that connection; it does not settle the disputed identity of the removed branches.
